body:
In just two years, people have created 70 million projects with Lovable, turning their ideas into businesses, solutions for their communities, and new ways of working inside some of the world’s largest companies. What began as a way to build software by describing an idea has become a way to act on entrepreneurial ambition, whether you’re starting a business or changing one from within.

There’s more to that story than one anniversary post can capture. So we’ve gathered perspectives from across Lovable, alongside new research and stories from the people using it, to reflect on what these two years have made possible and where we go next.

Here’s what you’ll find below:

• Two years of Lovable: Our latest milestones and stories of people creating businesses and changing how their companies work.

• New research: What holds people back from acting on their ideas, and how those who have made something feel about the future.

• A letter from our CEO and Cofounder, Anton Osika: On choosing optimism, finding your people, and shaping the world around you.

• Maryanne Caughey, Chief People Officer, in Fortune : How leaders can give employees the freedom and authority to change their companies from within.

• The next chapter of Lovable’s product: How Lovable will help people operate and grow their businesses.

## Two years of Lovable: the numbers & the people

Our community has built 70 million projects with Lovable, with 1.2 million more built every week, fueling our vision of a world shaped by everyone in it. Lovable-built apps receive over 1 billion visits a month, and since Lovable Payments launched in April, people have received more than $20 million from their customers through apps they built with Lovable.

That shift is taking hold inside companies of every size:

• Viver de IA (Brazil): Founder Rafael Milagre built his education company with Lovable, including the CRM, finance tools, website, and AI sales workflows. The company has 54 people and 1,200+ clients, and is on track for ~$20M USD in revenue this year.

• Imaginary Space (United States): Harry McKay Roper grew up making video games and wanting to be a programmer, but an early agency internship burned him out and pushed him toward design instead. Lovable let him bring both skills back together—he’s since grown Imaginary Space from $5–10K/month to an 18-person agency with $1.2M ARR, 300+ client projects, and customers from Dude Wipes to the UK government.

• Nursa (United States): Nenad Ivanovic, VP of Product, built Nursa Study, a new product for nursing schools, in a weekend. The CEO, Curtis Anderson, then opened the building to all 200-plus employees, and the company is retiring 10 software systems.

• Pendo (United States): Trish LaPaglia, VP of Employee Experience, built the hub for Pendo’s 800-person company kickoff in a single weekend, helping the company avoid up to $25,000 in software and agency costs. Since then, nearly 300 employees have built 1,400+ apps in five months across People, Marketing, Sales, RevOps, and Customer Success.

## New research: what stands between an idea and making it real

A new survey commissioned by Lovable explores what holds people back and how those who have made something feel about the future.*

• People want to participate. Nearly two-thirds (65%) want to use new technology to make money or build something but don’t know where to begin. Nearly half (45%) say the more they follow news and social media about the future, the less able they feel to influence it.

• The best ideas often go unmade. 69% have an idea to solve a problem they know well. Among those respondents, 42% have never made it.

• Getting started is the biggest barrier. Respondents cite not knowing where to begin (31%), being unable to afford someone to build their idea (28%), and believing they need a technical person (19%). Only 15% cite not having time to learn.

• People who have made something report having greater hope for the future. Among those who have made something to solve a problem they know well, 85% feel hopeful about the future, compared with 72% of those who haven’t. Nearly half (47%) are very hopeful, compared with 28% of those who haven’t made something.

• Companies have an idea gap, too. Among business owners and senior leaders surveyed, 68% say a good idea at their company has been dropped or never built because no one with the right skills, time, or budget was available.

* About the research: Censuswide surveyed 2,000 U.S. respondents, including a minimum of 250 small business owners and 250 mid-market business leaders, between October 29 and November 4, 2026.

## Letter from Lovable’s CEO and Cofounder, Anton Osika

In his anniversary letter, Anton shares the habit that helped Lovable get this far and offers a message to anyone feeling stuck:

• Choose optimism. You don’t need to know an idea will work before you try. Optimism helps you learn from failure and keep going.

• Find your people. The best things often begin when you share an ambition and find others willing to pursue it with you.

• Create more than you consume. Make room for the ideas that excite you. Acting on one of them can have a ripple effect across an entire community.

Read Anton’s anniversary letter

## Maryanne Caughey, Lovable’s Chief People Officer, in Fortune

Maryanne’s essay in Fortune explores how leaders can help employees turn their expertise into improvements across a business.

• Hire for craftsmanship. Look for relentless curiosity and expert judgment in a candidate’s own field, since skill with the tools alone says little about who will build something useful. Then give new hires real work from day one.

• Let the people closest to the problem build the solution. Notice where you’ve become a gatekeeper, back your first movers, and pair that freedom with clear guardrails.

• Give permission to do things differently. Ask how work should be done in the first place, shorten the distance between an idea and a decision,

وجمعت الشركة في منشورها أبحاثًا جديدة وقصص مستخدمين ورسالة من مؤسسها ومديرها التنفيذي أنطون أوسيكا.

• يُبنى 1.2 مليون مشروع جديد أسبوعيًا على المنصة.

• تتجاوز زيارات التطبيقات المبنية عبر Lovable مليار زيارة شهريًا.

• منذ إطلاق Lovable Payments في أبريل، حصل المستخدمون على أكثر من 20 مليون دولار من عملائهم عبر تطبيقاتهم.

• شركة Viver de IA البرازيلية بنت أدواتها (إدارة العملاء والمالية والموقع وسير المبيعات) عبر Lovable، ولديها 54 موظفًا وأكثر من 1200 عميل، وتتوقع إيرادات بنحو 20 مليون دولار هذا العام.

• وكالة Imaginary Space الأمريكية نمت إلى 18 موظفًا وإيراد سنوي متكرر بقيمة 1.2 مليون دولار وأكثر من 300 مشروع.

• يتضمن المنشور أيضًا بحثًا عن العوائق التي تمنع الناس من تنفيذ أفكارهم، ومقالًا عن المرحلة القادمة من المنتج لمساعدة الناس على إدارة أعمالهم وتنميتها.

تُظهر هذه الأرقام كيف يتحول بناء البرمجيات بالوصف النصي إلى وسيلة فعلية لريادة الأعمال.
